dataset_family: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative): 811 MCI participants, data 2005-2023, screening GDS-15 <= 5 and at least three GDS-15 assessments within five years
method_family: Longitudinal k-means clustering (R kml) of repeated GDS-15 into three trajectory classes, then sex-stratified linear mixed-effects models of MMSE/CDR-SB/ADAS-Cog-13/FAQ slopes and sex-stratified Cox models of MCI-to-dementia conversion, adjusted for age, education, APOE e4 and baseline GDS-15. Same evidence type as P-26 (ADNI GDS-15 trajectory classes predicting conversion), though P-26 used GBTM with a landmark design
same_sample_or_cohort_as: P-26 (ADNI; the row's counter-evidence study; both analyse ADNI MCI participants with repeated GDS-15, so participant overlap is very likely)
what_it_shows: In men with MCI, mildly and rapidly increasing depressive-symptom trajectories predicted steeper MMSE decline and higher conversion risk than consistently low symptoms (HR 1.59 and 2.69); in women neither trajectory was associated with decline or conversion (HR 1.37 and 1.25, ns). Baseline GDS-15 entered as a covariate did not predict MMSE slope in either sex once trajectory class was in the model. No brain measure, and every participant has MCI.
why: Wang et al., Alzheimer's Dement 2025;21:e70548. The PDF title and authors match the summaries.md block and the map entry. As a SUPPORTER of the Table A1 row the paper fails. Its primary result is positive severity-grading of conversion in men: the rising-symptom classes carry ordered hazards (1.59, then 2.69), which is the P-26 side of the row ('a monotone, dose-dependent relation of a ... depressive-symptom trajectory to conversion in ADNI'), not the supporter sentence ('continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'). It therefore belongs with P-26 as counter-evidence, and since it is also ADNI it adds no dataset family to that side. Its null elements do not rescue a support verdict: (a) the women's null concerns trajectory classes, not a continuous severity score, and is a subgroup result; (b) the baseline GDS-15 x time coefficient for MMSE slope is null (men 0.037, p 0.441; women 0.052, p 0.387), but it concerns cognitive decline rather than conversion or brain measures, it is estimated net of trajectory class (the classes differ in baseline GDS, 1 vs 2 vs 4), and baseline GDS is range-restricted to 0-5 by the entry criterion; (c) the baseline-GDS hazard ratio in the Cox models is in Table S4, which is not in the extract, so the authors' statement that trajectory 'rather than their baseline levels' was associated with dementia risk rests on their sentence. Other limits: the trajectory window (five years of GDS) overlaps the outcome window, so rising symptoms may partly reflect incipient dementia (P-26 used a landmark design to separate them); B and C did not differ significantly from each other on MMSE slope; no clinical depression diagnosis. It does not test the first clause (all MCI) or the brain limb. The 'divided' framing gains a within-study sex split from this paper, but a single study cannot demonstrate a corpus division, and the row's supporter sentence is contradicted in men. Independence: ADNI, the same family as P-26, P-731 and P-770; no shared authors evident (P-26's block names only 'Ding et al.'); no overlap with P-643, P-647, P-788 or P-974. Not a preprint. Symbols in quotes are transliterated to ASCII (<=, x for the interaction sign, - for minus).

quotes.quote: Data used in the preparation of this article were obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (adni.loni.usc.edu).

While the ADNI study enrolled only participants without clinical depression (defined as GDS-15 total score <=6) at the screening visit, we adopted a more conservative threshold (GDS-15 <=5) based on prior research to further exclude individuals with potential subclinical depressive symptoms.

we used longitudinal assessments of the GDS-15 over a 5-year follow-up period from all 811 MCI participants as the input variable in the k-means longitudinal clustering analysis using the R package "kml."
Cluster A: consistently low symptoms (n = 505, 62%), (2) Cluster B: mildly increasing symptoms (n = 250, 31%), and (3) Cluster C: rapidly increasing symptoms (n = 56, 7%).
Due to overlapping 95% CIs between Clusters B and C, these two groups did not exhibit significant differences in cognitive decline rates.

In men, compared to Cluster A, both Cluster B (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.59, 95% CI = 1.1-2.31, p = 0.014) and Cluster C (HR = 2.69, 95% CI = 1.4-5.15, p = 0.003; Table S4 in supporting information; Figure 3A) showed significantly elevated risks of dementia conversion. In contrast, depressive symptom trajectories were not significantly associated with dementia risk in women (Cluster B: HR = 1.37, 95% CI = 0.86-2.18, p = 0.2; Cluster C: HR = 1.25, 95% CI = 0.56-2.81, p = 0.6; Table S4, Figure 3B).

A, Association of depressive symptom trajectory with the risk of progression from MCI to dementia in men (x2 = 7.3, p = 0.03). B, Association of depressive symptom trajectory with the risk of progression from MCI to dementia in women (x2 = 0.5, p = 0.8).

our results indicated that the trajectory (i.e., time-varying pattern) of depressive symptoms, rather than their baseline levels, was associated with cognitive decline and dementia risk, particularly among men with MCI.
Third, the absence of baseline clinical depression was defined as a GDS-15 score <=5, rather than through a standardized clinical evaluation, which could introduce potential misclassification bias.
